Source: Arthur Collins, “The Duelist: a chaotic non-player character who likes to make people pay,” Dragon #73 (May 1983), p.7-9. Restated in plain words; the numbers follow the article.

As long as there has been one-on-one fighting, there have been experts who sell their skill at it. Mercenaries are something else: they fight as part of a troop, and most are no better than 0-level fighters. Winning fight after fight one-on-one takes more than a soldier has. The experts in single combat became duelists: the Roman gladiators, the fencing teachers of the Renaissance who taught young nobles to duel and live, and the hired swords of every age (hired guns in the Old West). The duelist makes a living by selling his skill in single combat.

Who becomes a duelist

Most duelists are common-born. Serfs never get the chance to learn arms, and nobles who take up arms usually become fighters or paladins. Some duelists are lower class, like the gladiators, perhaps because they fell foul of the law. Some are minor nobles, younger sons of younger sons with no inheritance and no wish to be soldiers. Some are loners or outcasts whose only fame is their skill with a blade.

Alignment and the duelist's code

Duelists have little use for law as a principle, whether the law is good, bad or neutral. Their trade is often illegal (though lawmen sometimes hire them), and they see life as “me against you,” not “us against them.” Most duelists are careful to keep their contracts, but that is professional pride, not lawfulness. Besides, an unreliable duelist gets no work.

The duelist's code mocks the knight's. A knight fights to do justice, plays fair, and belongs to a brotherhood sworn to protect the community. A duelist values skill over justice: if his conscience calls him a hired killer, he tells himself he is only doing his job (and doing it well). Like a knight, a duelist won't take unfair advantage of an opponent, but a knight does it to be fair and a duelist does it to protect his reputation. That is why a duelist won't use poison or flaming oil in a fight; those are for cheap assassins and stupid tavern brawlers, and using them would show a lack of skill and courage. The duelist is a loner, judged by what he alone has done.

So people fear, admire and avoid the duelist, and brag about knowing one, all at once. He is hero and villain both. Many duelists run fencing schools, which is a very respectable trade.

The duelist

  • Minimum ability scores: strength 9, intelligence 10, dexterity 15, constitution 9. Dexterity 17 or more gives +10% to experience earned; constitution gives hit point bonuses as for fighters.
  • Race: human or half-elf.
  • Hit dice: d12. Spells: none. Highest level: 15th (Grand Fencingmaster).
  • Armor: leather. Shield: none.
  • Weapons: dagger, scimitar (cutlass, sabre), quarterstaff, bastard sword, broad sword, long sword, short sword. Oil: no. Poison: no.
  • Attacks per round: 1/1 at levels 1-4, 3/2 at 5-9, 2/1 at 10-14, 5/2 at 15.
  • Weapon proficiencies: 3 at first, 1 more every 3 levels; −2 when not proficient.
  • Alignment: neutral good, neutral evil, chaotic good, chaotic evil, chaotic neutral or true neutral.

¹ Only duelists with 17+ dexterity can attain this level or higher. ² Only duelists with 18 dexterity can attain this level or higher.

  • There can be any number of Grand Fencingmasters, unlike the top levels of the assassin, druid and monk classes.
  • A duelist can have no henchmen before 7th level.
  • Of all fighter encounters in a city or town, 5% (1 on a d20) will be a duelist.

Experience

  • Duelists are often hired to kill people, usually by “calling out” the target. Duelists charge about what assassins do, and earn experience for the fee.
  • A duelist also earns experience from the Assassination Experience Points table for every foe he beats in single, open combat. The foe must be armed with a weapon, not only natural weapons as many monsters are.
  • “Open” means one-on-one with no surprise used by the duelist. It doesn't have to be in public or a formal challenge through seconds. A fight with any surprise by the duelist earns nothing from that table, unless the victim surprised the duelist. The DM rules on any doubtful case.

Hit dice

A d12 doesn't mean duelists are huge brutes. As the DMG says (p.82), hit points stand for both the body's toughness and a growing skill in combat, including a sixth sense for danger. In a long fight, losing hit points means getting tired more than getting cut, until one clean thrust can kill. A duelist's tricks, skill and stamina are better than other fighters', and the d12 shows that. A 10th level duelist averages more hit points than a 10th level fighter, so he can outlast a less skilled opponent one-on-one.

Surprise

A duelist is surprised only on a 1 on a d6. His code makes him dislike attacking by surprise in a one-on-one fight, but he is no fool: staying alive matters more than honor, and surprise isn't forbidden.

Bonuses against weapons

Against opponents armed with weapons (other than missiles), the duelist gets a bonus to armor class for his skill at parrying. He also gets a bonus to hit and damage (the “combat bonus”) against an opponent using a hand-held weapon, and a bigger one if the opponent uses the same weapon he does:

LevelAC bonusCombat bonusCombat bonus vs. same weapon
1-3+1+1+1
4-6+2+1+2
7-9+3+2+3
10-12+4+2+4
13-15+5+3+5

As a fighter

Duelists use the fighter's combat and saving throw tables, follow the fighter's rules for psionics and magic items, and count as fighters for anything not covered here.

Morale

Fighting size S or M humanoids hand to hand, the duelist and his companions get +10% to morale. The companions get it only if they know he is a duelist.

Parrying the death blow

  • When a weapon hit would take the duelist to 0 hit points or less, he gets a saving throw vs. death. If it succeeds, he takes no damage.
  • The second time in the same melee (not the same round), before he has healed any hit points, a successful save halves the damage (or leaves him at 1 hit point, if that is what it takes to keep him alive).
  • No third save in the same melee until he has had some hit points restored.
  • It works only against hand-held weapons used by creatures that use weapons: a minotaur's axe or a hill giant's club, yes; a dragon's bite, a pseudo-dragon's sting or a scythe-blade trap, no.

When it can be used. The parry comes into play once the duelist is low enough that the opponent's most possible damage in one blow could kill him. That is the weapon's highest damage plus all the opponent's damage bonuses. When the opponent hits, the duelist may try the parry before the damage dice are rolled.

Example. An opponent with strength 18/03 and a +1 long sword can do up to 12 points (8 for the sword, +1 for the magic, +3 for strength). Once the duelist is at 12 hit points or less, he may try the parry against this opponent after a successful “to hit” roll and before damage. At 5 hit points or less he must try it, because the opponent's least possible damage is 5 (1 for the sword, +1, +3).

While the opponent's least possible damage is lower than the duelist's hit points, the duelist can choose whether to try. It's a last-ditch trick, and he might save it for one more round. Against several opponents he may have to pick which equally deadly blow to parry, since he can't try it twice in a round.

Two weapons

Duelists take 1 point less penalty for off-hand attacks when fighting with two weapons. But they fight that way only against other two-weapon humanoids or ordinary monsters. Their code forbids using two weapons to gain an advantage over an opponent with one, except when their life is at stake.

Fear

Duelists save against fear attacks at +2.

Identifying magic weapons

From 10th level, a duelist has a 5% chance per level to identify the magic properties of a weapon his class can use (one try per weapon per level).

From 10th level (Fencingmaster), a duelist may open a fencing school. It must be in a large town or city, with enough supplies and room for the training. The school must employ a swordsmith. The Fencingmaster then attracts students.

What a Fencingmaster turns out aren't necessarily duelists: being one takes more than fighting skill. His customers are young men who want to be good at dueling but may never be able to become duelists. Where a gentleman is expected to handle arms (even if he plainly can't), the school is a clubhouse, gym, betting parlor and gossip shop all in one. The Master is a man of reputation, dangerous to cross, who can shut you out of much of society just by barring you from his hall. He has no place in society himself (being low-born and working for a living), yet holds one of the keys to its door, like the keeper of the most fashionable inn. And as at an inn, there is no better place to hear certain kinds of news.

Students

  • Hiring a Fencingmaster to teach costs 200 gp a month, one month at a time.
  • Each month of training gives the student a cumulative 10% chance of gaining +1 to hit with one particular weapon the Fencingmaster uses, to at most 60%. The dice are rolled once, at the end of the training. The training can't be broken up by adventuring. If the roll fails, the training starts over.
  • A student who has gained +1 with a weapon (a long sword, say) can't gain more with it by further study, however long, but can gain the +1 with other weapons through more lessons.
  • A Fencingmaster can teach up to 30 students at once. If he goes adventuring for more than 3 days in a month, his students' training is interrupted too long, and he loses the income from them.
  • Number of students: roll 5d6, and add one for every 3 points of the Fencingmaster's charisma, to at most 30.
  • Unlike fighters, Fencingmasters gain no followers at name level (10th), even with a school.

Reputation

Word about duelists gets around, more so as they get better. Most duelists know of other duelists of equal or higher level nearby. Sometimes a duelist calls out another just to prove himself. Grand Fencingmasters, and many other famous duelists with high charisma, are more often honored than challenged.

What the module does

  • Adds the class Duelist (Dragon #73): the article's experience and titles to 15th, d12 hit dice (10, then +2 hit points a level), the fighter attack table, saves and constitution bonus, exceptional strength, and attacks per round as printed.
  • Proficiency: 3 weapons, 1 more every 3 levels, −2 when not proficient (as printed).
  • The attack dialog asks what the opponent is using: a hand-held weapon (combat bonus), the same weapon (the bigger bonus) or something else (none). The armor class bonus is noted on the card but not applied, since it depends on the attacker.
  • The Duelist tab rolls the death blow parry (save vs. death, counting parries in the melee), weapon identification and school students.
  • The Record tab shows notes, which never block anything: ability minimums, race, the dexterity needed for 9th and 10th level, a lawful alignment, more than one class, and armor or weapons not allowed.

Choices made here

  • Nonweapon proficiency slots are a fighter's; the article doesn't give them.
  • The combat bonus is offered only on the duelist's melee attacks, not his missile attacks.
  • Not applied automatically: the armor class bonus, surprise, +2 vs. fear, morale, the two-weapon reduction.
